```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Willingness to pay is better evidenced for A. Several sourced incumbents charge money for this exact capability: Maskwire sells 'Alias replies' at $3/mo, addy.io includes it on $1–4 tiers, and SimpleLogin Premium runs about $3–4/mo. In B, the Reddit-specific competitors (SlopSieve, Redd-Eye) are all free. Its only paid anchor, ReviewGuard at $1.99/mo, covers Google Maps and TripAdvisor reviews, not Reddit.",
    "A's demand evidence is specific to the feature. Three sourced forum threads on Zoho, Apple and Microsoft describe the exact failure the product fixes: replies going out from the wrong alias. B's quotes show general frustration with bots. They do not show that anyone wants, would install, or would pay for a client-side filter.",
    "A has a well-specified, deterministic core: map the recipient header to the outgoing From address. B depends on noisy AI-detection heuristics. B's own brief says these already misflag real users, which risks harming the core use case and adds ongoing tuning work.",
    "B carries platform risks that A largely avoids. It depends on third-party DOM structures and Reddit's tolerance under its ToS. A can choose a plugin or extension surface that avoids both the proxy credential burden and its GDPR exposure.",
    "Both ideas face entrenched competition with sub-$5 price ceilings. A's competitors at least confirm that a paying market exists. B's free, open-source competitors actively suppress any price."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's demand evidence is the Reddit quotes ('People are sick and tired of bots...', 'the increase in bots has led me to take time away from reddit') plus a Slashdot summary of a Financial Times interview. Together they establish only that bot spam exists and annoys people. None of it shows demand for, or willingness to pay for, a filtering extension. The CEO statement is secondhand and confirms the problem, not a market.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-low confidence. Both briefs describe commoditized markets with free or bundled incumbents, very low prices, and no install or revenue data. A wins mainly because its competitors prove people pay for the feature. That same fact means a standalone A must win customers away from established bundled products. Neither brief presents strong evidence that a first paying customer within 90 days is likely."
}
```
